To keep them on the run, the Bushmen planted buteas—a kind of mimosa with a poisonous poison in its leaves and thorns—near their huts and hunt stations.
Butea and mangroves are usually found in tropical forests in low-lying areas.
A huge butea tree is already flowering outside the main entrance.

The plant is used by Indians for medicine, especially against lung complaints and as an antifungal to cure sore throats and for other mouth diseases and tooth pain, and is also used in toothpasting powder and toothbrushes along with butea gum which resembles rosin and has a bitter taste.
They include krafta (gum tragacanth), butea gum, tragacanth and other gums, and some resins.

Butea gum was one of the first resins to be discovered by Europeans. Its history goes back to the time of the Aztecs in Mexico, whence it came to the West Indies and from there travelled up into the southern states. Other common names for the gum are Butea gum, Panama gum, Peru gum, and pitch resin.
The resin is also called butea gum.
A similar resinous secretions are also found in Butea and other tropical timbers.
Butea gum (the sap of the tree) is also used as a medicine to soothe irritated throat and mouths.
The sap is collected in bamboo tubes and left to harden. This solidified sap is known locally as buthea gum, which is a resinous substance obtained by distillation of the dried sap.
The gum known as butea or buttersweet from Butea monosperma is also used as a thickener in glue preparations.
Butea gum is not the only natural adhesive used to make gum balls; there are also gum rosin and copal, both made by heating vegetable resin with steam.
